title: The calcium nobody corrected
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module’s KDIGO 2017 and KDOQI 2020 statements and grades; no doses are given. The unit’s protocol, formulary and the attending nephrologist decide every order.

monitor.meds: Calcium carbonate at bedtime; others not asked

intro:
You are the internal medicine resident covering a hemodialysis unit in Pasig on a Saturday. Mrs. Lorna Aquino, 58, a retired public school teacher, has dialyzed three times a week for three years. Two months ago she broke her wrist in a minor fall at home.

The intern, Dr. Jasper Lim, reads out her monthly results: calcium 10.3 mg/dL with albumin 3.2 g/dL, phosphate 6.8 mg/dL, and intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) 85 pg/mL, with an assay upper normal limit (ULN) of 65 pg/mL. A year ago her PTH was 240 pg/mL. Alkaline phosphatase is normal. She takes calcium carbonate “two tablets before sleeping.” The intern says, “Calcium is upper normal, so that’s fine.”

n1.prompt: What do you tell the intern?

choices.text: Agreed; calcium is fine. Focus on the phosphate, which is the real problem here.
choices.feedback: A measured calcium with a low albumin underestimates the free calcium. Uncorrected, it hides a hypercalcemia that changes the whole plan.
choices.then: The charge nurse asks about the albumin. You correct the calcium and ask about every supplement. She also takes calcitriol capsules from an old prescription and a calcium with vitamin D tablet she saw advertised on television.

vitals.meds: CaCO₃ at bedtime + calcitriol + over-the-counter calcium/vitamin D

choices.text: Correct it for albumin (about 10.9 mg/dL, high), line up three results, list her products.
choices.feedback: 10.3 + 0.8 × (4.0 − 3.2) is about 10.9 mg/dL. KDIGO 2017 asks you to read phosphate, calcium and PTH together as trends (not graded), and the intern’s product list is where the cause is usually found. Three dated results with the PTH assay limit, and every calcium and vitamin D product she takes, including over-the-counter ones.
choices.then: Dr. Lim finds two more products: calcitriol capsules she still buys from an old prescription, and a calcium with vitamin D tablet she saw advertised on television.

vitals.meds: CaCO₃ at bedtime + calcitriol + over-the-counter calcium/vitamin D

choices.text: Order an ionized calcium before anyone decides anything, since total calcium is unreliable.
choices.feedback: Ionized calcium is more reliable in very sick or very low-albumin patients, where your laboratory offers it. Here the corrected value already answers the question, and the product history matters more.
choices.then: You correct the calcium yourself and ask about every supplement. She also takes calcitriol capsules from an old prescription and a calcium with vitamin D tablet she saw advertised on television.

vitals.meds: CaCO₃ at bedtime + calcitriol + over-the-counter calcium/vitamin D

n2.scene: Her PTH has fallen from 240 to 85 pg/mL over a year, now about 1.3 times the assay’s upper limit, while her calcium has climbed.
n2.prompt: How do you read it, and what do you propose to the attending?

choices.text: Add a calcimimetic to help bring the phosphate down and keep the PTH from rising again later.
choices.feedback: Calcimimetics lower PTH, and her PTH is already too low. Pushing it lower deepens the oversuppression, and calcimimetics do not remove phosphate.
choices.then: The attending declines the calcimimetic and holds the calcitriol and the over-the-counter tablet.

vitals.plan: Calcitriol and over-the-counter calcium/vitamin D held

choices.text: A low PTH is good news for her bones and vessels. Continue everything as it is.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2017 suggests keeping PTH on dialysis at about 2 to 9 times the assay’s upper limit (2C). Below that, bone turnover can stall, and a calcium load goes to vessels instead of skeleton. Her fracture fits.
choices.then: At rounds the attending holds the calcitriol and the over-the-counter tablet.

vitals.plan: Calcitriol and over-the-counter calcium/vitamin D held

choices.text: Oversuppression and possible adynamic bone: propose cutting her calcium and vitamin D.
choices.feedback: Too little PTH is the second wrong turn. Calcium carbonate, calcitriol and an extra supplement together suppress the glands and leave bone inactive. KDIGO 2017 suggests avoiding hypercalcemia in adults (2C). PTH below the KDIGO dialysis range with high calcium and a recent fracture.

vitals.plan: Calcitriol and over-the-counter calcium/vitamin D held

n3.scene: Her phosphate is still 6.8 mg/dL. She takes the calcium carbonate at bedtime.
n3.prompt: What binder plan do you propose?

choices.text: Keep the calcium carbonate, but move it to mealtimes so more of it binds phosphate.
choices.feedback: Mealtimes are right: a binder works only on the phosphate in the food it meets. But it still adds calcium to a patient who is hypercalcemic with suppressed PTH.
choices.then: The attending moves the binder to meals and asks you to discuss a non-calcium binder with the family.

vitals.plan: Binder with meals; non-calcium option discussed

choices.text: An aluminum hydroxide antacid daily: it is cheap and has no calcium.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2017 recommends avoiding long-term aluminum-containing binders (1C), one of its strongest statements. Aluminum accumulates in bone and brain.
choices.then: The pharmacist flags the order. You discuss a non-calcium binder with the family instead.

vitals.plan: Binder with meals; non-calcium option discussed

choices.text: A non-calcium binder if affordable, less calcium binder, and the cost talk in the chart.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2017 suggests restricting calcium-based binder doses in adults (2B). In a meta-analysis of 11 trials, non-calcium binders were associated with lower mortality, but the trials were small and open label. A plan she cannot buy every month is not a plan. Taken with meals; restrict the calcium-based binder.

vitals.plan: Binder with meals; non-calcium option discussed

choices.text: Double the calcium carbonate to bring the phosphate down faster before her next laboratory test.
choices.feedback: More calcium carbonate means more absorbed calcium in a patient who cannot store it. That is the opposite of the KDIGO direction.
choices.then: The attending declines and asks you to discuss a non-calcium binder, taken with meals.

vitals.plan: Binder with meals; non-calcium option discussed

n4.scene: She tells you what she eats: pandesal with corned beef from a can in the morning, instant pancit canton at lunch, and a cola in the afternoon. “Should I stop eating meat and fish to lower the phosphorus?”

choices.text: Keep protein at about 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg; swap the processed foods; teach “phos” on labels.
choices.feedback: On dialysis she needs more protein, not less (KDOQI 2020). Additive phosphate in processed food and cola is absorbed most completely. In a cluster trial, additive education lowered phosphate by 0.6 mg/dL, a surrogate, at almost no cost. Fresh fish or chicken instead of canned meat and instant noodles, water within her fluid allowance instead of cola.

choices.text: Refer her to the dietitian and leave the advice to them, since diet is their field.
choices.feedback: The dietitian is the right partner, but she asked you directly. One sentence on keeping protein and one on additives answers her fear and sends her to the dietitian with the right question.
choices.then: The dietitian keeps her protein at 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg and teaches her to read labels for “phos.”

choices.text: Yes, cut meat and fish; get her protein from rice.
choices.feedback: Starving a dialysis patient of protein invites protein-energy wasting. The phosphate is better lowered by food choice, binders with meals and enough dialysis time.
choices.then: The dietitian corrects the advice: protein stays at 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg, and the processed foods go.

n5.scene: Her calcium is back in range and her PTH has risen into the KDIGO range. Then, at a Saturday session, the nurse shows you two hard, purplish patches on her thighs. She winces when the sheet touches them.

choices.text: Photograph them and discuss at Monday rounds with the wound care team.
choices.feedback: Photographs help, but painful purplish lesions in a dialysis patient need attending input today. Two days can matter.
choices.then: The nurse asks you to call. The attending comes in to see her.

choices.text: Start an antibiotic for cellulitis and send her home.
choices.feedback: Treating it as simple cellulitis risks missing calciphylaxis, which carries high mortality and needs the attending urgently.
choices.then: Before she leaves you reconsider and call the attending, who comes in to see her.

choices.text: A topical steroid, and review in a month.
choices.feedback: A month is far too long. Painful violaceous lesions on the thighs of a patient with a history of calcium loading may be calciphylaxis.
choices.then: The charge nurse is uneasy and asks you to call. The attending comes in to see her.

choices.text: Call the attending now: this may be calciphylaxis.
choices.feedback: New, very painful, purplish lesions on the thighs or abdomen of a dialysis patient are on the module’s stop-and-call list. Call per unit protocol, but always ask the attending nephrologist for guidance.

end.title: The next weeks
end.text: The attending saw her the same day and took over the workup and plan for the skin lesions. You documented her calcium and vitamin D history, the oversuppressed PTH a year earlier, and the changes since. She now brings every bottle to clinic, and the intern keeps a dated table of her calcium, phosphate, PTH with its assay limit, and alkaline phosphatase.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Correct the calcium and line up the trend before you act on any single value, with the PTH assay limit written beside each PTH.
  • Too little PTH is harm too. Below about 2 times the upper limit on dialysis (2C), with high calcium, think oversuppression and cut the calcium and vitamin D load.
  • Spare calcium: restrict calcium-based binders (2B), avoid hypercalcemia (2C), never use aluminum long term (1C), and take any binder with meals.
  • On dialysis, keep protein at 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg and lower phosphate by swapping processed foods.
  • Painful purplish skin lesions on dialysis: call the attending now.
